title: Living ashtpadi 22
tomorrow: Ashtpadi 23, salok: the ointment of wisdom

lines: A BOY, A ROBE, A FLOWERING BUSH.
cards: Sikhs tell a story about the seventh Guru, Guru Har Rai, when he was a boy. Walking through a garden in a long, flowing robe, he brushed past a flowering bush, and a few petals fell to the ground.
His grandfather, Guru Hargobind, saw it and told him gently that a robe that wide must be carried with care. The boy, the story goes, was so moved that he kept that care all his life.

teach.b: Here's the twenty-second ashtpadi in brief. God is the thaakur, the Master, of jeea jant, every living being.

The One is spread through them all, dwelling ghat ghat, in every heart, and sustaining each creature with its daily bread. Put together, one plain line: everything alive is His. Living it starts with how we touch things.
The story of Guru Har Rai is passed down in Sikh tradition rather than recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib, but its point fits the ashtpadi exactly.
If every living thing belongs to the One, a flower isn't just scenery and an animal isn't just a resource.
They're in someone else's care, and we're walking through the garden.

Sikh tradition remembers Guru Har Rai as a lover of gardens and animals, and as someone who kept medicines to give to the sick, including, by many accounts, the son of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, whose family were no friends of the Gurus.
Everything alive is His, including the people we'd rather not help.
In practice, this can be very small: watering the office plant everyone forgets, driving a little slower past the park, asking how the elderly neighbor's dog is doing. None of it is grand.
But each small act says: this life isn't mine to waste. It belongs to the One who is spread through all.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-second ashtpadi hear that every living being belongs to the One, and Sikh tradition remembers Guru Har Rai for his care of gardens, animals and the sick.

games.q: the son of a family hostile to the Gurus is sick, and you have the medicine. what does the tradition remember Guru Har Rai doing?
games.why: by many accounts he sent the medicine. everything alive is His, including the people we'd rather not help.

practice: Yesterday was food; today is care.

Tend one living thing slowly, a plant that needs water, litter on the path outside, a tired person at home who'd like a cup of tea, as if it belonged to someone you love, because in the ashtpadi's picture it does; or, if nothing is nearby, picture the one you'll care for later.
If you pray, say Waheguru as you tend it.

wordCard.voice: Jeea, living beings, those with life and breath: every jeea has the same Master, the same indwelling Light, the same Feeder; so every living thing is handled with care.

carryVoice: Your line: everything alive is his. Seven days, from the stillness to the garden. See you tomorrow.
